title: Cr.A No. 197-A of 2024 with MR No. 05-A of 2024 Syed Mubarak Shah Vs. The State
text:
Judgment Sheet
IN THE PESHAWAR HIGH COURT,
ABBOTTABAD BENCH
(JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT)
Cr.Appeal No. 197-A/2024
With Murder Reference No. 05-A/2024
Syed Mubarak Shah……………Appellant.
Vs.
The State……………….Respondent.
Present:
M/s Abdul Saboor Khan and Waqar
Ahmed Khan, Advocates for the
appellant.
Mr. Shoaib Ali, Assistant AG for the
State.
Mr. Muhammad Arshad Awan, Advocate
for the complainant/respondent.
Date of hearing: 19.05.2026
JUDGEMENT
*******************
AURANGZEB, J.- This single judgment shall
dispose of Criminal Appeal No.197-A/2024 filed
by appellant Syed Mubarak Shah, connected
Criminal Appeal No.201-A/2024 filed by appellant
Yaqoob Khan as well as Murder Reference No.05-
A/2024 sent by the learned trial Court for
confirmation of death sentence awarded to
appellant Syed Mubarak Shah. Since all these
2
matters arise out of one and the same judgment,
therefore, the same are being decided through this
consolidated judgment.
2. Briefly stated, the prosecution case as set forth
in the FIR is that on 13.07.2021 at about 05:25
p.m., complainant/injured Faizan Zeb along with
injured Danish reported the occurrence to local
police at Emergency Ward, King Abdullah
Teaching Hospital, Mansehra. It was alleged that
after finishing their work near Thandi Khoi, while
they were returning to their houses and reached
near a shop situated at Thandi Khoi, accused
Mubarak Shah along with co-accused persons was
standing there. Upon seeing the complainant party,
the accused persons allegedly started altercation
and abuses. In the meanwhile, accused Mubarak
Shah allegedly picked up a glass bottle and struck
the same on the head of injured Danish. Thereafter,
accused Yaqoob Khan allegedly took out a pistol
and fired at Danish causing firearm injury on his
left thigh. Subsequently, accused Mubarak Shah
allegedly drew out his pistol and fired at
complainant Faizan Zeb causing firearm injury on
3
the right side of chest and abdomen. The
occurrence was witnessed by Mohsin and Asad.
Initially, case under Sections 324/34 PPC was
registered, however, after death of injured Faizan
Zeb, Section 302 PPC was incorporated in the FIR.
3. After completion of investigation, challan was
submitted before the learned trial Court. Formal
charge was framed against the accused persons to
which they pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. In
order to substantiate the charge, prosecution
produced as many as sixteen witnesses. Statements
of accused persons under Section 342 Cr.P.C. were
recorded wherein they denied prosecution
allegations and professed innocence. However,
they neither opted to appear as witnesses under
Section 340(2) Cr.P.C. nor produced any evidence
in defence. Upon conclusion of trial, learned trial
Court convicted and sentenced the appellants in
the following manner:-
Appellant Syed Mubarak Shah was convicted
under Section 302(b) PPC and sentenced to death
for committing qatl-i-amd of deceased Faizan Zeb.
He was also directed to pay compensation
amounting to Rs.500,000/- to the legal heirs of
4
deceased under Section 544-A Cr.P.C. and in
default whereof, to further undergo six months
simple imprisonment. He was further convicted
under Sections 324/34 PPC and 337-F(iii)/34 PPC
and sentenced accordingly.
Appellant Yaqoob Khan was convicted under
Section 302(b) PPC read with Section 34 PPC and
sentenced to imprisonment for life besides payment
of compensation under Section 544-A Cr.P.C. He
was also convicted under Sections 324 PPC and
337-F(iii) PPC and sentenced accordingly. Benefit
of Section 382-B Cr.P.C. was extended to both the
appellants.
4. We have heard learned counsel for the parties
at considerable length and have meticulously gone
through the entire available record with their able
assistance.
5. The unfortunate occurrence in the instant
matter is not disputed. It stands admitted from the
record that deceased Faizan Zeb sustained firearm
injury during the occurrence and subsequently
succumbed thereto, whereas injured Danish also
sustained firearm injury on his left thigh. The
prosecution case mainly rests upon the dying
declaration of deceased Faizan Zeb embodied in
the Murasila/FIR, testimony of injured witness
5
Danish (PW-13), ocular account furnished by
Mohsin Ali (PW-14), medical evidence, recoveries
and forensic report.
6. At the very outset, before adverting to the
ocular account, it would be advantageous to
discuss the evidentiary value of the FIR lodged by
deceased Faizan Zeb himself, which subsequently
assumed the character of dying declaration within
contemplation of Article 46 of the Qanun-e-
Shahadat Order, 1984. The record reveals that the
occurrence took place on 13.07.2021 at about
05:00 p.m., whereas the matter was reported to
police at 05:25 p.m. at King Abdullah Teaching
Hospital, Mansehra through PW-3 Muhammad
Riaz ASI. Thus, the report was lodged with utmost
promptitude and without any delay whatsoever.
The prompt reporting of occurrence excludes
possibility of deliberation, consultation or
fabrication and lends strong assurance to
truthfulness of prosecution version.
7. The prosecution evidence consistently
establishes that immediately after sustaining
firearm injury, deceased Faizan Zeb along with
6
injured Danish was shifted to hospital in a taxi
where his statement was recorded by PW-3
Muhammad Riaz ASI. Injured Danish (PW-13),
who himself sustained firearm injury during the
occurrence and also attested the report as witness,
categorically deposed before the Court that after
the occurrence he along with injured Faizan Zeb
travelled in the same taxi towards hospital and
there, deceased Faizan Zeb himself narrated the
occurrence to PW-3 in his presence, whereafter he
attested the report as marginal witness. His
testimony on this aspect remained consistent and
confidence inspiring throughout.
8. Likewise, PW-3 Muhammad Riaz ASI
unequivocally stated that injured Faizan Zeb was
conscious and in senses at the time when he
reported the matter to him. He further proved
Murasila/report Ex.PW-3/1 along with injury
sheets Ex.PW-3/2 and Ex.PW-3/3 pertaining to
deceased Faizan Zeb and injured Danish
respectively. He further deposed that injured
Danish attested the report as witness. The witness
remained steadfast during lengthy cross-
7
examination and nothing favourable to defence
could be extracted from his testimony.
9. The prosecution version regarding physical
and mental condition of deceased Faizan Zeb at
relevant time also finds full support from medical
evidence. PW-11 Dr. Usman medically examined
both injured persons immediately after occurrence
and specifically stated that although injured Faizan
Zeb was in critical condition, however, he was
conscious. During cross-examination, the witness
replied to the suggestion of learned defence
counsel that even if lung of injured had been
damaged, medically such injured could still speak.
Thus, the medical evidence completely negates
defence contention that deceased Faizan Zeb was
incapable of making statement.
10. Before placing reliance upon the statement of
deceased Faizan Zeb embodied in the
Murasila/FIR, it would be appropriate to discuss
the legal principles governing evidentiary value of
dying declaration. A dying declaration is an
exception to the general rule excluding hearsay
evidence and has been made admissible under
8
Article 46 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984
on the principle that a person standing at the brink
of death is not likely to falsely implicate an
innocent person. The law consistently recognizes
that when a statement is made by a deceased
person relating to cause of his death or
circumstances resulting in his death, such
statement becomes relevant and admissible
provided the same inspires confidence and is
proved in accordance with law.
11. The august Supreme Court of Pakistan in the
case of “Abdul Khaliq versus The State” reported
as 2021 SCMR 325 held that where a deceased
was conscious and medically fit to make statement
and the same was recorded immediately after
occurrence, such dying declaration carries
substantial evidentiary value and can safely be
relied upon if surrounding circumstances establish
its truthfulness. Likewise, in “Majeed versus The
State” reported as 2010 SCMR 55 and “Nazeer
Khan versus The State and another” reported as
2019 SCMR 1308, the august Supreme Court
recognized the evidentiary sanctity of dying
9
declaration where circumstances establish that the
same was made voluntarily and truthfully.
12. It is equally settled that a dying declaration
need not necessarily be made under immediate
expectation of death. In “Wazir Gul versus The
State” reported as 1976 SCMR 471 and “Zarif
Khan versus The State” reported as PLD 1977
Supreme Court 612, the august Supreme Court
held that expectation of immediate death is not a
sine qua non for admissibility of dying declaration.
Similarly, FIR lodged by injured person himself,
who subsequently succumbs to injuries sustained
during occurrence, can legally be treated as dying
declaration if proved in accordance with law.
Reference in this regard may be made to 1990
SCMR 588, PLD 2003 Supreme Court 635,
PLD 2006 Supreme Court 186 and 2011 PCr.LJ
1455.
13. The principles for determining genuineness
and reliability of dying declaration have
consistently been elaborated by superior Courts. In
the celebrated judgment rendered by the Hon’ble
Lahore High Court in “Taj Muhammad and
10
others versus The State” reported as PLD 1960
Lahore 723, it was held that if a dying declaration
is found to be genuine and true, it can by itself
form sufficient basis for conviction. It was further
held that some of the principal tests for judging
veracity of dying declaration are whether
intrinsically it rings true, whether there existed any
chance of mistaken identity, whether the maker of
declaration was physically and mentally capable of
making statement, whether the statement was free
from prompting or tutoring from outside influence
and whether the same remained consistent with
other evidence and circumstances of the case.
14. Likewise, this Court in “Zabta Khan versus
The State” reported as PLD 1963 (W.P.)
Peshawar 66 adopted and reiterated the above
principles. Similarly, in “Abdur Rahim versus The
State” reported as 1997 PCr.LJ 1274, the criteria
for evaluating evidentiary worth of dying
declaration was further elaborated in the following
terms:-
(i) Whether there was no chance of mistaken
identity;
11
(ii) Whether deceased was capable of making
statement;
(iii) After how much time of sustaining injury the
statement was made;
(iv) Whether the statement rings true;
(v) Whether it was free from prompting or outside
influence; and
(vi) Whether deceased was a person of
questionable character.
15. The august Supreme Court of Pakistan in
“Muhammad Afzal versus Faqir and others”
reported as PLD 1984 Supreme Court 375 further
observed that merely because injured person had
sustained serious injuries, it cannot automatically
be presumed that he was incapable of making
statement, particularly where medical evidence
establishes that injured remained conscious and fit
to communicate. The august Supreme Court
emphasized that medical opinion and surrounding
circumstances are of decisive importance while
assessing truthfulness of dying declaration.
16. Similarly, in “Abdul Razik versus The State”
reported as PLD 1965 Supreme Court 151, it was
held that though dying declaration is admissible
under law, however, its acceptance or rejection
12
ultimately depends upon judicial evaluation based
upon ordinary human conduct, surrounding
circumstances and intrinsic worth of statement
itself.
17. Examined in the light of the above settled
principles, the dying declaration embodied in the
Murasila/FIR in the present case fully satisfies all
legal requirements necessary for placing reliance
upon the same. Firstly, there existed no possibility
of mistaken identity because parties were
admittedly known to each other prior to
occurrence. Secondly, the statement was made
immediately after occurrence at the earliest
possible opportunity leaving hardly any time for
consultation, deliberation or fabrication. Thirdly,
the prosecution evidence consistently establishes
that deceased Faizan Zeb was conscious and
mentally fit to make statement at the relevant time.
PW-3 Muhammad Riaz ASI categorically stated
that injured Faizan Zeb himself narrated the
occurrence to him at hospital, while PW-11 Dr.
Usman specifically deposed that although injured
was in critical condition, however, he was
13
conscious. Even during cross-examination, the
doctor stated that despite injury to lung, an injured
person could still speak. Fourthly, the statement
made by deceased Faizan Zeb intrinsically rings
true and remained fully consistent with the ocular
account subsequently furnished by injured Danish
(PW-13) and eyewitness Mohsin Ali (PW-14). The
role attributed by deceased to accused Mubarak
Shah and accused Yaqoob Khan remained
consistent throughout prosecution evidence and
materially corresponded with medical as well as
forensic evidence available on record. Fifthly,
there is nothing on record suggesting that the
statement was outcome of tutoring, prompting or
external influence. On the contrary, the promptness
with which the report was lodged itself excludes
possibility of concoction.
18. The deceased in his dying declaration
specifically narrated that accused Mubarak Shah
fired at him causing firearm injury on his chest,
whereas accused Yaqoob Khan caused firearm
injury to injured Danish. This narration was
subsequently corroborated by injured witness
14
Danish (PW-13), who also stated that accused
Mubarak Shah first inflicted bottle blow upon him
whereafter accused Yaqoob Khan fired at him
causing firearm injury on his thigh and
subsequently accused Mubarak Shah fired at
deceased Faizan Zeb. Likewise, eyewitness
Mohsin Ali (PW-14) furnished substantially same
account of occurrence. Thus, the dying declaration
not only remained intrinsically trustworthy but also
received independent corroboration from ocular,
medical and forensic evidence.
19. In the circumstances discussed above, we are
of the considered view that the statement of
deceased Faizan Zeb embodied in the
Murasila/FIR constitutes a truthful, voluntary and
reliable dying declaration within contemplation of
Article 46 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984
and the same can safely be relied upon as a
substantive piece of evidence against the accused
persons.
20. The dying declaration of deceased Faizan
Zeb further receives substantial corroboration from
testimony of injured witness Danish (PW-13). It is
15
by now well settled that testimony of an injured
witness carries its own sanctity and evidentiary
worth because his presence at the place of
occurrence stands established through injuries
sustained by him during the same transaction. An
injured witness ordinarily would not substitute
actual offender and falsely implicate an innocent
person at the cost of allowing real culprit to
escape.
21. Injured Danish (PW-13) furnished a
straightforward, natural and confidence inspiring
account of occurrence. He categorically deposed
that on the day of occurrence he along with
deceased Faizan Zeb and witness Mohsin was
returning from work and when they reached at
Thandi Khoi, accused Mubarak Shah and accused
Yaqoob Khan started altercation with them.
According to him, accused Mubarak Shah picked
up a bottle and struck the same on his head.
Thereafter, accused Yaqoob Khan took out a pistol
and fired at him causing firearm injury on his left
thigh. Subsequently, accused Mubarak Shah drew
16
out pistol and fired at deceased Faizan Zeb causing
firearm injury on the right side of his chest.
22. The testimony of injured Danish remained
consistent on all material particulars regarding
date, time, place, manner of occurrence and
identity of assailants. Despite lengthy and
searching cross-examination, no material
contradiction, improvement or infirmity could be
pointed out in his statement. His presence at the
place of occurrence stands conclusively
established through firearm injury sustained by
him during same occurrence, which was medically
examined immediately thereafter.
23. The august Supreme Court of Pakistan in the
case of “Ansar and others versus The State”
reported as 2023 SCMR 929 held that testimony
of injured witness supported by medical evidence
clearly establishes his presence at place of
occurrence and such testimony ordinarily carries
strong probative force. Similarly, in “Altaf
Hussain versus The State” reported as 2025
SCMR 1427, it was held that injured witness
enjoys a special status because injury sustained by
17
him during occurrence constitutes an
unimpeachable circumstance regarding his
presence at crime scene.
24. The prosecution version further finds
corroboration from independent ocular witness
Mohsin Ali (PW-14), who was specifically named
in the FIR as witness of occurrence. He fully
supported prosecution case and deposed that on
relevant day he along with deceased Faizan Zeb
and injured Danish was returning from work and
reached at Thandi Khoi where altercation took
place between parties. He further stated that
accused Mubarak Shah inflicted bottle blow upon
Danish whereafter accused Yaqoob Khan fired at
Danish causing firearm injury on his leg and
subsequently accused Mubarak Shah fired at
deceased Faizan Zeb causing firearm injury on
right side of chest.
25. PW-14 Mohsin Ali further deposed during
cross-examination that both injured persons were
shifted to hospital in a single taxi. This aspect
materially corroborates testimony of injured
Danish regarding shifting of injured persons to
18
hospital immediately after occurrence and
recording of report by deceased Faizan Zeb at
hospital. The ocular account furnished by PW-13
and PW-14 remained in complete harmony with
each other and no material discrepancy could be
pointed out therein.
26. The ocular account furnished by prosecution
witnesses further finds complete support from
medical evidence. PW-11 Dr. Usman medically
examined injured Danish as well as injured Faizan
Zeb immediately after occurrence and noted
firearm injuries on their respective persons. Injury
sustained by injured Danish on left thigh fully
corresponds with ocular account regarding role
attributed to accused Yaqoob Khan. Likewise,
firearm injury sustained by deceased Faizan Zeb
materially supports prosecution case that accused
Mubarak Shah fired at him during occurrence.
27. Subsequently, PW-7 Dr. Ijaz Ahmad
conducted postmortem examination upon dead
body of deceased Faizan Zeb and opined that death
occurred due to firearm injury damaging vital
organs resulting in hemorrhagic shock and
19
hypoxia. The medical evidence thus fully
corroborates prosecution version regarding seat of
injury, nature of weapon used and manner of
occurrence.
28. Apart from ocular and medical evidence,
prosecution case also receives substantial
corroboration from forensic and recovery
evidence. The investigation officer during
inspection of place of occurrence recovered blood-
stained earth along with three empties of .30 bore
pistol and four empties of 9 mm pistol from spot.
Thereafter, .30 bore pistol allegedly used by
accused Mubarak Shah was recovered on his
pointation on 18.07.2021, whereas 9 mm pistol
was recovered from accused Yaqoob Khan on
05.08.2022. Both the recovered weapons along
with crime empties were sent to Forensic Science
Laboratory for examination.
29. The report of Forensic Science Laboratory
returned positive wherein empties recovered from
place of occurrence were found to have been fired
from respective recovered weapons. The positive
forensic report constitutes an important
20
corroborative piece of evidence connecting
accused persons with commission of offence.
Similarly, blood-stained articles secured from spot
and clothes of injured/deceased were also taken
into possession during investigation and same
further supported prosecution case.
30. It is significant to observe that defence failed
to establish any previous enmity, ill-will or ulterior
motive on part of deceased or injured witnesses for
falsely implicating accused persons in such a
serious offence while sparing actual culprits. The
prosecution witnesses remained consistent, natural
and confidence inspiring throughout. Their
testimony finds full support from prompt FIR
treated as dying declaration, medical evidence,
recovery of crime empties, positive forensic report
and surrounding circumstances of case. Hence, we
are satisfied that prosecution has successfully
established participation of accused persons in
occurrence to extent of their respective roles
beyond shadow of reasonable doubt. Reference
may be made to the case of “Ali Taj and another
Vs. The State” reported as 2023 SCMR 900 and
21
“Muhammad Shabbir and others Vs. The State”
reported as 2020 SCMR 1206.
31. However, despite the fact that prosecution
succeeded in proving occurrence and participation
of accused persons, the crucial question requiring
determination is whether the case falls within
ambit of premeditated murder attracting extreme
penalty or whether mitigating circumstances are
available warranting lesser sentence. Admittedly,
prosecution itself alleged that occurrence had taken
place all of a sudden on a trivial issue. The FIR
itself reveals that altercation and abuses started
between parties at spot and thereafter unfortunate
occurrence took place. No previous motive or
enmity has been attributed by prosecution. Entire
occurrence appears to have taken place at spur of
moment without preplanning or premeditation.
32. It is also noteworthy that appellant Syed
Mubarak Shah is not shown to be previous convict
nor there is any evidence on record demonstrating
his involvement in previous criminal cases of
similar nature. Thus, possibility that he acted under
sudden provocation and emotional excitement
22
cannot be ruled out. It is settled principle of
criminal jurisprudence that where occurrence takes
place at spur of moment without premeditation and
mitigating circumstances are available, normal
penalty of death may be substituted with
imprisonment for life.
33. We are therefore of the considered view that
present case is not one of extreme penalty.
Occurrence admittedly took place suddenly during
altercation. There was no previous motive, no
preplanning and no evidence of calculated design.
Hence, sentence of death awarded to appellant
Syed Mubarak Shah under Section 302(b) PPC
warrants reduction to imprisonment for life. In the
case of “Muhammad Shabbir and others Vs. The
State” reported as 2020 SCMR 1206, the
honourable Supreme Court held that;
“In such like cases where the murders
are committed as revenge depends upon
human physiology. The human being a
creature of the environment; therefore,
he is governed by the background of the
society from where he hails. Although
this aspect do not cover the doctrine of
provocation still the area and other
23
antecedent of persons are relevant factor
while taking into account which might be
suggesting for a moment where revenge
can be regarded as mitigating
circumstances, however, the question of
sentence in each criminal case definitely
has direct nexus with the particular
circumstances of the said case. This
principle was considered and relied upon
by salutary judgment titled "Ajun Shah v.
The State" (PLD 1967 Supreme Court
185). The learned High Court while
handing down the judgment impugned
before us has already taken care of all
established principles of law and
converted the sentences of each
appellant from death to imprisonment for
life which seems to us appropriate and in
accordance with law.”
34. The next important question pertains to
applicability of Section 34 PPC. Upon careful
scrutiny of prosecution evidence, we are unable to
persuade ourselves that prosecution succeeded in
establishing shared common intention between
appellants within contemplation of Section 34
PPC. Occurrence erupted suddenly during
altercation. Role attributed to each accused is
distinct and individual. Prosecution evidence does
24
not establish any preconcert or prior meeting of
minds. Above all, the accused charged alogn with
the present appellants have been acquitted of the
charge by the learned trial Court through the same
judgment. In such circumstances, principle of
individual liability would apply and each accused
would be liable only for his own overt act.
35. So far as appellant Syed Mubarak Shah is
concerned, specific firearm injury causing death of
deceased Faizan Zeb is attributed to him.
Therefore, his conviction under Section 302(b)
PPC is maintained. However, for reasons already
discussed, sentence of death awarded to him is
reduced to imprisonment for life. He shall also pay
compensation of Rs.500,000/- to legal heirs of
deceased under Section 544-A Cr.P.C. and in
default whereof, shall further undergo simple
imprisonment for six months.
36. However, since common intention has not
been established, therefore, conviction and
sentence of appellant Syed Mubarak Shah under
Sections 324/34 PPC and 337-F(iii)/34 PPC are
hereby set aside.
25
37. So far as appellant Yaqoob Khan is
concerned, admittedly no injury to deceased
Faizan Zeb has been attributed to him. His
conviction under Section 302(b) PPC read with
Section 34 PPC is therefore not sustainable and
same is hereby set aside. Nevertheless, prosecution
evidence consistently establishes that appellant
Yaqoob Khan caused firearm injury to injured
Danish. His conviction under Section 324 PPC is
therefore maintained. However, sentence awarded
to him under Section 337-F(iii) PPC as Ta’zir is
set aside, whereas conviction to extent of payment
of Daman is maintained.
38. Consequently, Criminal Appeal No.197-
A/2024 filed by appellant Syed Mubarak Shah is
partly allowed in the manner that while
maintaining his conviction under Section 302(b)
PPC, his sentence of death is reduced to
imprisonment for life along with compensation of
Rs.500,000/- payable to legal heirs of deceased
under Section 544-A Cr.P.C. and in default
whereof, to further undergo simple imprisonment
for six months. His conviction and sentence under
26
Sections 324 PPC and 337-F(iii) PPC are set aside.
Benefit under Section 382-B Cr.P.C. is extended to
him.
39. Criminal Appeal No.201-A/2024 filed by
appellant Yaqoob Khan is also partly allowed. His
conviction and sentence under Section 302(b) PPC
read with Section 34 PPC are set aside. His
sentence under Section 337-F(iii) PPC as Ta’zir is
also set aside; however, conviction under Section
337-F(iii) PPC to extent of Daman is maintained.
Similarly, his conviction and sentence under
Section 324 PPC are maintained. Benefit under
Section 382-B Cr.P.C. is also extended to him.
40. Resultantly, Murder Reference No.05-
A/2024 is answered in negative.
Announced:
19.05.2026.
J U D G E
J U D G E
/*Tufail. P.S*/
Hon’ble Mr. Justice Syed Mudasser Ameer
Hon’ble Mr. Justice Aurangzeb
headnote:
(a) A dying declaration constitutes an exception to the general rule excluding hearsay
evidence and is admissible when it relates to the cause of death or the circumstances
leading to the death of the maker. The underlying rationale is that a person facing death is
unlikely to falsely implicate another. Such a statement becomes relevant and can be relied
upon provided it is proved in accordance with law and inspires confidence. The evidentiary value of a dying declaration is particularly significant where the deceased
was conscious, mentally fit, and capable of making a statement. A statement recorded
promptly after the occurrence and made voluntarily, without any external influence, carries
substantial probative value and may form the basis of conviction if found truthful and
reliable. It is well settled that a dying declaration does not require an immediate expectation of
death to be admissible. Likewise, where an injured person lodges an FIR and subsequently
dies from the injuries sustained in the occurrence, such FIR may legally assume the
character of a dying declaration if properly proved. The reliability of a dying declaration is assessed on several established considerations,
including whether the maker correctly identified the accused, was physically and mentally
capable of making the statement, made it within a reasonable time of sustaining injuries,
and whether the statement appears truthful, voluntary, and free from prompting, tutoring, or
outside influence. Consistency with the surrounding circumstances and other evidence on
record is also an important factor. The character and credibility of the deceased may
further be considered while evaluating its evidentiary worth. The mere fact that a person sustained serious injuries does not automatically render him
incapable of making a reliable statement. Where medical evidence and surrounding
circumstances demonstrate that the injured person remained conscious and fit to
communicate, the statement may safely be relied upon. Ultimately, the acceptance or
rejection of a dying declaration depends upon its intrinsic reliability, the surrounding
circumstances, and its conformity with ordinary human conduct. Applying these settled principles, the dying declaration contained in the Murasila/FIR in the
present case fulfils the legal requirements of admissibility and reliability and is therefore
capable of being safely relied upon as evidence. (b) It is by now well settled that testimony of an injured witness carries its own sanctity and
evidentiary worth because his presence at the place of occurrence stands established
through injuries sustained by him during the same transaction. An injured witness ordinarily
would not substitute actual offender and falsely implicate an innocent person at the cost of
allowing real culprit to escape. that injured witness enjoys a special status because injury
sustained by him during occurrence constitutes an unimpeachable circumstance regarding
his presence at crime scene. (c) The prosecution case was proved through consistent ocular, medical, forensic, and
recovery evidence. The injured witness and an independent eyewitness, both present at
the scene, gave a coherent account of the occurrence, stating that a sudden altercation led
to the use of firearms, resulting in injuries to one person and the death of another. Their
testimony remained consistent and was corroborated by the immediate shifting of the
injured persons to the hospital. The ocular account was fully supported by medical evidence, which confirmed firearm
injuries on both the injured witness and the deceased. The post-mortem examination
established that the deceased died from a firearm injury to a vital organ, consistent with the
prosecution's version of events. The prosecution case received further corroboration from the recovery of crime empties,
blood-stained articles, and firearms recovered from the accused. Forensic examination
confirmed that the crime empties had been fired from the recovered weapons, thereby
connecting the accused with the offence. No evidence of prior enmity or motive for false implication was produced by the defence.
The prosecution evidence remained natural, consistent, and confidence-inspiring, and was
supported by the dying declaration, medical evidence, forensic findings, and surrounding
circumstances. Consequently, the participation of the accused in the occurrence was
established beyond reasonable doubt. However, the evidence also showed that the incident occurred suddenly during an
altercation on a trivial matter, without prior motive, planning, or premeditation. In view of
these mitigating circumstances, the case was held not to warrant the death penalty, and
the sentence was reduced to imprisonment for life. The evidence further failed to establish any common intention or prior concert between the
accused as required under Section 34 PPC. Since the occurrence was spontaneous and
the role of each accused was separate and distinct, the principle of individual liability was
applied, making each accused responsible only for his own overt act.
